title: Milestone: Energy to Information
objective: After this level you can connect electricity, engines and communication into one story of modern technology.
summary: Chapter 1 used electricity for power; Chapter 5 used it for messages. A signal carries information in its pattern, and Chapter 1's parts sit inside every device.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Follow one current from power to message.
cards.body: Chapter 1 put electricity to work: heating a filament until it glows, spinning a motor. This chapter asked the same current to carry words, voices and pictures. Put the two side by side, and one story appears.

cards.headline: From a pile of metal discs to a phone in your hand

events.label: Volta's pile, the first reliable battery
Morse's telegraph carries "What hath God wrought!"
Marconi picks up radio dots across the Atlantic
Cooper makes the first handheld cell phone call

cards.headline: Same electricity, two jobs
cards.body: Power is about how much energy flows. A signal is about the pattern. The telegraph's pattern was on and off: dots and dashes. The telephone's was a current that rose and fell like a sound wave. Radio sent patterns through the air as waves, and television sent the brightness of each spot. A tiny current can carry a big message, because what matters is its shape.

cards.headline: Milestone: energy to information
learned: How the same current that lights a lamp can carry messages, because information lives in its pattern.
How the telegraph and telephone send words by wire, and how radio carries sound with no wire at all.
How cameras and screens break a picture into dots, and why red, green and blue are enough to fool the eye.
Why cell networks use small, low-power cells, and why radio and TV have no single inventor.

questions.prompt: Printing look-back: about how many books did Europe have by 1500, after 50 years of presses?

options.label: A few thousand
options.rationale: That was before printing.

options.label: About 180
options.rationale: Far too few for a whole continent.

options.label: About 9 billion
options.rationale: A thousand times too many.

questions.explanation: Britannica counts more than 9 million books in Europe by 1500, up from thousands of hand-copied ones.

questions.prompt: Telephone credit look-back: whose work did the US House of Representatives honor in a 2002 resolution?

options.label: Elisha Gray
options.rationale: Gray filed a caveat in 1876, but the 2002 resolution honored someone else.

options.label: Thomas Watson
options.rationale: Watson was Bell's assistant on the first call.

options.label: Samuel Morse
options.rationale: Morse built the telegraph.

questions.explanation: The 2002 House resolution honored Antonio Meucci, who had filed a telephone caveat but couldn't pay the $10 fee to keep it after 1874.

questions.prompt: Energy to information: in a communication signal, what carries the message?

options.label: The total energy the current delivers
options.rationale: A tiny current can carry a big message.

options.label: How hot the wire gets
options.rationale: Heat is waste, not the message.

options.label: The color of the wire's insulation
options.rationale: Insulation just keeps the current in.

options.label: The pattern of the current or wave

questions.explanation: A signal carries information in its pattern: on-off pulses for the telegraph, a current shaped like sound for the telephone, a varied wave for radio.

questions.prompt: Screen look-back: which subpixels glow together to make a pixel look white?

options.label: Red and green only
options.rationale: Red and green light make yellow.

options.label: None of them
options.rationale: All off looks black.

options.label: Blue only, at full brightness
options.rationale: That just looks blue.

questions.explanation: Mixing light adds up: red, green and blue together look white to the eye's three kinds of cones.

questions.prompt: Energy to information: which Chapter 1 idea is at work in both a telegraph receiver and a smartphone speaker?

options.label: Energy turning mostly into heat
options.rationale: That's Level 5's old bulb, not these devices.

options.label: Chemicals storing energy for later
options.rationale: That's the battery's job.

options.label: A current making a magnetic field
A steady magnet making current in a coil
options.rationale: A still magnet induces nothing (Level 8).

questions.explanation: Both use a current to make a magnetic field: it pulls the telegraph's stylus and moves the speaker's coil.

questions.prompt: Energy to information: what happens inside your phone's lithium-ion battery while it charges?

options.label: Fresh electrons are poured into it
options.rationale: A battery never runs out of electrons.

options.label: Current in reverse runs the reaction backward, storing energy
The battery spins like a small generator
options.rationale: Nothing spins in a battery.

options.label: Its liquid is swapped for new chemicals
options.rationale: The same chemicals are restored.

questions.explanation: Charging drives current through the battery in reverse, running the chemical reaction backward so it stores energy again (Level 6).

questions.prompt: Cell network look-back: you walk from one cell into the next mid-call. What does the network's central controller do?

options.label: Drops the call and dials it again
options.rationale: Handoff happens without a noticeable break.

options.label: Tells your phone to raise its power
options.rationale: The network moves the call instead.

options.label: Switches your call to a landline
options.rationale: It stays on the cellular network.

options.label: Reroutes the call to the new cell's base station

questions.explanation: A handoff: the controller automatically moves the call from the old cell's base station to the new one.
